key_terms.meaning: A named, persistent unit of bytes kept on secondary storage; the OS identifies it by name, not by address.
Metadata stored per file: name, type, size, location, owner, permissions and timestamps.
Also called random access: block n is read after computing its address, without reading blocks 1 to n−1 first.
A file whose data is a table mapping file names to file entries or inode numbers.
Index node: the Unix on-disk record that holds a file's attributes and block pointers, but never its name.
The directory in the existing tree where a separate file system is attached; the old contents of that directory become hidden.
Marking a whole file or a byte range so other processes cannot read or write it; advisory locks need cooperating processes, mandatory locks are enforced by the OS.
A kernel layer that offers one set of calls (open, read, write) above many different concrete file systems.
The per-file-system record describing block size, free-block structure, inode table location and mount state.
A file occupies one run of consecutive blocks; the directory entry holds the start block and the length.
Each block of a file holds a pointer to the next block; the directory entry holds only the first and last block numbers.
All block numbers of a file are kept in one index block, and the directory entry points to that index block.
A free-space map with one bit per block: 1 means free, 0 means allocated.
The CPU repeatedly reads a device status register in a loop until the device shows the work is finished.
A hardware signal that makes the CPU stop its current work and jump to a handler when a device needs service.
A controller moves a whole block between device and main memory without per-byte CPU work; the CPU gets one interrupt at the end.
Kernel code that knows one device's registers and commands, and turns generic I/O requests into them.
Holding data in a kernel memory area while it moves between device and process, to match differing speeds and transfer sizes.
The time to move the disk head to the target cylinder; a full stroke from the innermost to the outermost cylinder costs the most.
The head sweeps from one end of the disk to the other serving requests in order, then reverses, like a lift.

takeaways: A file is a name, a set of attributes and a stream of bytes; the directory holds the name and the control block holds the rest.
The access method decides whether reading block n costs one disk read or n disk reads.
Directory structures trade search speed against the ability to share one file under several paths.
Mounting joins separate file systems into one tree without copying any data.
The VFS gives one interface, and every concrete file system supplies the operations behind that interface.
The allocation method fixes three things at once: random-access speed, external fragmentation and the largest possible file.
Polling burns CPU cycles, an interrupt costs a mode switch, and DMA moves a block with a single interrupt at the end.
Disk scheduling exists because seek time dominates on rotating media, and SSTF can starve a far-away request.
bank_note: Long answers here usually pair one numerical part — head movement, bitmap size or pointer overhead — with a written comparison of design choices, so practise both halves before the exam.

bank.q: Define a file. List the attributes an operating system keeps for each file and state what each attribute is used for.
outline: File = named, persistent collection of bytes on secondary storage
Name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, owner, timestamps
Name lives in the directory; the rest in the file control block or inode
Why the OS separates name from the control block (renaming, sharing)

bank.q: Explain sequential access and direct access. Give one workload where each is the better choice.
outline: Sequential: read/write in order, OS keeps a current-position pointer
Direct: compute block address, read that block alone
Cost per access in disk reads for each
Example: compiler log or media file for sequential; database index for direct
Indexed access as a variant built on direct access

bank.q: Describe tree-structured and acyclic-graph directories. Why does the acyclic graph need reference counts or garbage collection?
outline: Single-level and two-level limits: naming collisions, no grouping
Tree: one parent per file, absolute and relative path names
Acyclic graph: shared files and directories, links
Deleting a shared file: dangling pointer problem
Reference count per file, or cycle detection and garbage collection
Traversal cost of path lookup in each structure

bank.q: Compare polling, interrupt-driven I/O and DMA. State the cost the CPU pays in each case.
outline: Device registers: data, status, control
Polling: busy loop, wasted cycles, simple
Interrupt: CPU notified, handler runs, mode switch and handler overhead
DMA: controller moves block, one interrupt per block
When each is preferred (fast device, slow device, large transfers)

bank.q: Explain the layers of I/O software from the user call down to the device, and name the data structures passed between them.
outline: User-level I/O library, system call interface
Device-independent kernel I/O: naming, buffering, caching, scheduling
Device driver layer, interrupt handler
Hardware: controller and device registers
Structures: file descriptor, open file table entry, buffer, request block

bank.q: A disk head rests on cylinder 50. The request queue is 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190. Compute the total head movement for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN (moving towards larger cylinder numbers first) and C-SCAN.
outline: FCFS: serve in arrival order, sum absolute differences from 50
SSTF: always nearest request, show the sequence and the total
SCAN: go up to 199, then down to the smallest pending, count the sweep
C-SCAN: sweep up to 199, jump back to 0, sweep up again, add the return jump
State the final totals with cylinder units

bank.q: A file has 100 blocks on a disk with 4 KB blocks; a block pointer takes 4 bytes. Compute the pointer overhead of linked allocation. Then find how many block numbers one index block can hold.
outline: Linked: one pointer per block = 4 bytes × 100 blocks
Effective data per block drops from 4 KB, so more blocks are needed
Index block capacity = 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024 pointers
One index block therefore addresses 1024 blocks = 4 MB
Extend to two-level indexing for larger files

bank.q: A 1 TB disk uses 4 KB blocks. Find the size of its bit-vector free-space map. Compare with a linked free list that stores one 4-byte pointer per free block when the disk is half empty.
outline: Number of blocks = 1 TB ÷ 4 KB = 2²⁸ blocks
Bit vector = 2²⁸ bits = 2²⁵ bytes = 32 MB
Half-empty disk: 2²⁷ free blocks × 4 bytes = 512 MB of list pointers
Conclusion: bitmap is far smaller, but needs a linear scan; list gives first free block quickly

bank.q: A machine keeps /home on a separate partition. Explain step by step what happens when that partition is mounted on /home, and what a process sees at that path before and after the mount.
outline: Mount system call: device plus target directory
Kernel reads the superblock, checks the file-system type, calls its mount routine
A mount record is added to the mount table
Old contents of /home become hidden but are not deleted
Path lookup now crosses into the new file system at that point
Unmount fails while files are still open there

bank.q: Trace what happens when a process calls read() on /home/user/data.txt, from the path name to the bytes arriving in the process buffer. Name every structure touched and say which layer owns it.
outline: System call trap, file descriptor looked up in the per-process table
Path resolution: root, each directory component, inode of each
VFS object for the mounted file system, then its own inode read
Permission check with owner and mode bits
Page cache lookup before any disk request
Block numbers from the inode, request sent to the block device layer
Driver programs DMA, device raises interrupt, handler wakes the process
Data copied from kernel buffer to user buffer, byte count returned

bank.q: Compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation on random-access speed, external fragmentation, file growth and pointer overhead. Recommend one for a database file and one for a log file that only grows.
outline: Contiguous: one seek for random block, external fragmentation, hard to grow
Linked: no external fragmentation, sequential good, random access costs n reads, pointer space per block
Indexed: random access in two reads, index block overhead, maximum file size limit
FAT as a linked variant with the pointer table in memory
Database file → indexed or contiguous; growing log → linked or indexed with extents

bank.q: Buffering and caching both hold data in memory. Analyse why a kernel needs both, and when double buffering changes throughput.
outline: Buffer: absorbs speed and size mismatch for one transfer
Cache: keeps a copy of data likely to be reused
Different lifetimes and different hit-rate aims
Double buffering: device fills one buffer while the process empties the other
Effect on a slow device feeding a bursty consumer
Cost: extra memory copies and memory pressure

bank.q: Evaluate SSTF against SCAN. Which one can starve a request and why? What does SCAN do to requests at the two ends of the disk, and how does C-SCAN fix it?
outline: SSTF picks nearest request, so a stream of near requests can starve a far one
SCAN is starvation-free within one sweep, models a lift
SCAN treats the two ends unevenly: the middle is served twice per sweep
C-SCAN returns without serving on the way back, giving uniform wait
LOOK and C-LOOK stop at the last request instead of the disk edge

bank.q: A file system must survive a power cut in the middle of a write. Evaluate the order in which the data block, inode and free-space bitmap should be written, and explain how a journal changes that order.
outline: Crash consistency: what state each partial write leaves behind
Write the data block before the inode that points to it, otherwise the inode points at garbage
Bitmap update must agree with the inode, or blocks leak or get double-allocated
Journal: write intent record, commit, then apply to the real structures
Recovery replays committed transactions only
fsck as the slower alternative that scans everything

glossary.def: A path that starts at the root directory and names every directory down to the file.
A path interpreted from the process's current working directory instead of the root.
A small integer a process uses to refer to an open file in later read, write and close calls.
Kernel table holding the offset and access mode of each open file, with a per-process table pointing into it.
A second directory entry that points to the same inode, so the file has one copy and two names.
A small file whose contents are a path name; the OS re-resolves that path when the link is opened.
A run of consecutive blocks recorded as one (start, length) pair inside an inode.
The smallest addressable unit on a disk platter, traditionally 512 bytes and now often 4096 bytes.
The set of tracks at the same radius on all platters, reachable without moving the head.
A contiguous region of a disk treated as an independent device that can hold one file system.
A file system that writes each metadata change to a log first, so recovery replays the log instead of scanning the whole disk.
A linked-allocation variant where all next-block pointers sit in one table kept in memory.
The first blocks of a partition, holding the code the firmware loads to start the operating system.
The wait for the spinning platter to bring the target sector under the head, 0 to one full rotation.
The time to move the requested bytes between disk and memory once the head is in place.
Holding complete jobs in a buffer, typically on disk, so a slow device such as a printer can work through them one at a time.
The kernel's memory copy of recently read file blocks, checked before any disk read is issued.
A scheme where device registers appear at ordinary memory addresses, so normal load and store instructions drive the device.
A table of handler addresses indexed by interrupt number, used to dispatch each interrupt quickly.
The electronics that accept block read and write commands, position the head and transfer data to memory.
The number the OS uses for a block on a device; the controller converts it to cylinder, track and sector.
Disk area holding pages pushed out of memory; space is allocated in whole pages, not by a general file system.
A call that puts the process to sleep until its data is ready, so the scheduler can run someone else meanwhile.
The in-memory copy of the superblock: block count, free-block count and pointers to free lists.
